Silicon photonic signal processors promise a new generation of signal pro-
cessing hardware with signiﬁcant advancements in processing bandwidth, low
power consumption, and minimal latency. Programmable silicon photonic
signal processors, facilitated by tuning elements, can reduce hardware
development cycles and costs. However, traditional programmable photonic
signal processors based on optical switches face scalability and performance
challenges due to control complexity and transmission losses. Here, we pro-
pose a scalable parallel signal processor on silicon for versatile applications by
interleaving wavelength and temporal optical dimensions. Additionally, it
incorporates ultra-low-loss waveguides and low-phase-error optical switch
techniques, achieving an overall insertion loss of 10 dB. This design offers low
loss, high scalability, and simpliﬁed control, enabling advanced functionalities
such as accurate microwave reception, narrowband microwave photonic ﬁl-
tering, wide-bandwidth arbitrary waveform generation, and high-speed par-
allel optical computing without the need for tuning elements calibration. Our
programmable parallel signal processor demonstrates advantages in both
scale and performance, marking a signiﬁcant advancement in large-scale, high-
performance, multifunctional photonic systems.
Silicon-based photonic signal processors have ushered in a new era of
signal processing, leveraging their expansive bandwidth, minimal
latency, low power consumption, and robust information security1–5.
Assisted by tuning elements, programmable photonic signal pro-
cessors can switch between different signal processing tasks, estab-
lishing a versatile hardware platform capable of addressing a wide
array of applications6–9. This versatility signiﬁcantly expands the
potential market and reduces unit costs10–13.
To date, various silicon programmable photonic signal processors
have been proposed. Intensive studies have focused on developing

Alternatively, parallel photonic signal processing using multi-
wavelength optical sources, such as multi-channel wavelength lasers
or frequency-comb lasers, offer substantial potential to extend signal

processing capabilities. Leveraging multiple dimensions of light,
including wavelength, amplitude, phase, and time delay, this approach
enables high-speed processing and simpliﬁed control for a wide range
of applications19–23. However, previous on-chip demonstrations have
shown limited performance due to restricted tunability of delays and
device scale19,21–24. For practical use, large dynamic ranges of delay are
highly desired as they allow longer time windows and more complex
signal processing. For instance, such capabilities are crucial for precise
phase adjustments and narrow-width beam steering ( ~ MHz beam
width) for spacecraft, satellites, and advanced auto-drive car sensing
systems3,25,26; they provide spatial separation for different parts of input
signals, enabling high-speed parallel-convolution calculations for large-
scale AI processors27. Moreover, they support trafﬁc congestion
management28, wider-width pulses generation29, narrow-band micro-
wave photonic ﬁlter30, and accurate measurements of distance, fre-
quency, or other physical parameters31,32 in advanced photonic
applications. However, conventional silicon photonic waveguides typi-
cally exhibit high propagation losses of 1-2 dB/cm, limiting long delays.
Efforts to reduce chip losses and extend delays have focused on opti-
mizing mode ﬁeld distribution and improving fabrication processes33,34.
Nonetheless, these methods may not fully align with current multi-
project-wafer
(MPW)
foundry
processes,
hampering
massive
production34. Recently, we proposed ultra-low-loss broadened silicon
waveguides, which are far beyond the singlemode regime and compa-
tible with standard foundry fabrication processes35. These waveguides
have losses as low as 0.14 dB/cm. Based on this technique, a 4-channel
chip-scale programmable photonic signal processor was realized,
enabling functions such as tunable time-delay (TDL) and microwave
photonic beamforming8. Additionally, broadened silicon photonic
waveguides have proven effective in enhancing fabrication tolerance
and minimizing random phase errors during light propagation36. This
allows to simplify the conﬁguration of large-scale programmable pho-
tonic signal processors, compared with other methods such as
improved processor architectures37 or self-conﬁguring algorithms7,38,39.
In this study, we propose a scalable programmable signal pro-
cessor on silicon for versatile optical and microwave photonic signal
processing by interleaving wavelength and temporal optical dimen-
sions. Our design integrates two 16-channel wavelength-division-
multiplexing (WDM)-based (de)multiplexers for wavelength selection
and amplitude control, and 6-bit TDLs for temporal signal manipula-
tion. The device enables parallel signal processing in each channel with
an overall loss depending only on a single channel, ensuring scalability
and effective management of complex tasks. We utilize ultra-low-loss
waveguide spirals with a broadened cross-section of 3 × 0.22 μm². The
phase shifters in the arms of the optical switches are widened to 2 µm
to achieve low random phase errors due to fabrication imperfections.
A pair of dual-elliptical rings (DERs) are used as WDM-based (de)mul-
tiplexers, carefully designed to maximize the free spectral range (FSR)
for broad optical bandwidths40. Our silicon photonic processor occu-
pies a chip area of about 14.05 mm², with each TDL channel offering a
tuning range from 0 to 201.6 ps. The waveguide propagation losses is
about 0.14 dB/cm, and the overall chip insertion loss is around 10 dB
including the ﬁber-chip coupling losses. This parallel signal processor
offers versatile high-performance functionalities, including accurate
microwave reception, narrowband microwave photonic ﬁltering, wide-
bandwidth arbitrary waveform generation, and high-speed parallel
optical computing. This work lays the groundwork for high-perfor-
mance, large-scale programmable photonic processors, poised to
revolutionize various optical applications and accelerate the devel-
opment of integrated photonics for the next generation.
Results
Design and fabrication
The proposed versatile parallel signal processor is illustrated con-
ceptually in Fig. 1a. The design enables parallel signal processing
through multi-channel, multi-wavelength, and multi-delay states
coordination. Multi-wavelength lasers or microcomb source serve as
the light source. Each wavelength is demultiplexed by an on-chip
wavelength-division demultiplexer based on ﬁrst DER array. The
demultiplexed signals are send to the TDL channel, where each chan-
nel can be tuned individually to control the delay (optically) /phase
(electrically) of the signals. At the output, delayed signals are routed
through optical switches. One output port is combined and amplitude-
controlled by the second tunable DER array, while another output port
is directly guided to the edge coupler array for detection. On the basis
of this approach, system-level demonstrations are presented for sev-
eral major integrated photonics ﬁelds that require ultra-wide band-
width, high-speed operation, and low power consumption, as shown in
the insets of Fig. 1a. These systems include: (a) Microwave beam-
forming reception is demonstrated with controllable steering angle
and beamwidth by tuning the delay, amplitude and channel number.
The beam achieves a 10.1° width with a wide ±75° angle range, facil-
itating accurate and wide-angle beam reception. (b) Narrow-band
microwave photonic ﬁlters with controllable FSR (5–34.3 GHz)/3-dB
bandwidth (3.4−11.9 GHz) is demonstrated. A continuous waveform
envelope arbitrary waveform at radio frequency (RF) of 312.5 GHz is
also demonstrated. (c) Parallel convolution-operation technology at
1.25 TOPs with conﬁgurable kernels is demonstrated. The maximum
number of processing channels (kernel size) is 16.
In this work, a 16-channel parallel signal processor is proposed and
demonstrated to implement this concept, and the chip layout is shown
in Fig. 1b It comprises 1 × 16 DER-based demultiplexer, optical-switch-
based 16 channels TDL, and a 16 × 1 DER-based multiplexers. The DERs
are connected in cascade to form the wavelength (de)multiplexers and
they are equipped with tuning elements to ensure wavelength align-
ment across channels for ﬂat optical ﬁltering and low-loss transmission.
Each TDL channel comprises a 6-bit digitally-TDL with 7 thermo-optic
switches based on MZIs, providing tunable time delays ranging from 0
to 201.6 ps (Ttotal) with a 3.2 ps step (Δτ). In order to conveniently test
individual channels and reduce the overall device loss, we used grating
couplers to test each channel separately (otherwise, more crossings
would be needed to use edge couplers). This architecture minimizes the
circuit footprint and heat dissipation, as detailed in Supporting Infor-
mation, Section S5. The chip was fabricated using a standard silicon
MPW foundry with a 220 nm-thick silicon core. The optical microscopy
image is depicted in Fig. 1c. More details about the fabrication method
can be found in Supporting Information, Section S1. The overall chip
footprint is 3.65 × 3.85 mm2. The fully-packaged chip with a thermo-
electric cooler (TEC) is shown in Fig. 1d, where all of the tuning units are
wire-bonded to a carrier printed circuit board and optical I/Os are
accessed with optical ﬁber arrays. All the tuning building blocks are
controlled by a programmable control circuit (PCC) for reconﬁguration.
Chip characterization
The major challenges for realizing large-scale processor are reducing
chip loss and programming complexity while maintaining a compact
footprint. In this work, we introduced high-performance components
to overcome this challenge. First, we utilized low-loss broadened sili-
con photonic waveguides with a compact Euler curve technique to
reduce the waveguide loss and improve the fabrication tolerance, as
shown in Fig. 2a. More details about the loss reducing method, Euler

15 time lower than that of singlemode waveguide (2 dB/cm). This
improved fabrication tolerance also enhances delay accuracy, as
detailed in Supporting Information, Section S3.4.
Secondly, we introduce calibration-free MZI optical switches with
broadened phase-shifters, so that the random phase imbalance is sig-
niﬁcantly reduced41,42. In this way, one realizes calibration-free MZI

Due to the calibration-free nature of the present MZI optical switches,

the large fabrication tolerance of the broadened waveguides, the delay
variation for different states across all channels remained below ±1 ps.
This feature offers promising applications in various ﬁelds, including
beamforming systems26, optical computing27, and optical buffers28.
The simulation results of large fabrication tolerance on different
applications are shown in Supporting Information, Section S3.5.
In addition, the DERs with adiabatically varied radii/widths
(Fig. 2d) are designed to shrink cavity length and reduce loss. This
design enables DERs to implement large bandwidth, ﬂat-top ﬁltering,
and large FSR for 16-channel wavelength (de)multiplexing. The details

Microwave photonic beamformer
In beamforming systems, both the transmitting and receiving ends can
share the same integrated photonic beamforming network chip25,26. In
this work, our processor is demonstrated within a receiving system
where RF signals received by multiple antennas are modulated onto 16
optical wavelengths. As shown in Fig. 3a, varying time delays are
applied to the optical signals, giving each RF signal an incremental
phase. The signals are then combined and restored to microwave
beams through a single PD. The PD should have a wide bandwidth and
sufﬁcient responsivity for the subsequent RF power meter to detect
the received signal accurately. At the receiver, constructive inter-
ference occurs for signals arriving from the desired direction, while
destructive interference occurs for signals arriving from other direc-
tions, allowing easy identiﬁcation of the signal direction. This
approach simpliﬁes the system design by avoiding the complexities
associated with a single continuous wavelength (CW) laser, such as
phase locking and synchronization. The measured phase responses for
6 delay states of all 16 channels are depicted in Fig. 3b, with the phase
delay normalized to the state with the shortest delay. The channel
delay measurement setup are shown in Supporting Information, Sec-
tion S2.1. Figure 3c illustrates the group delay derived from the fre-
quency derivative of the measured phase. The delay line offers a
relatively ﬂat delay tuning range from 0 to 201.6 ps across 0–40 GHz
frequency range. The average phase and delay responses (solid line) at
the same state are nearly overlapping with the measured data of 16
channels (shaded area), afﬁrming the large fabrication tolerance and
device uniformity of our processor. The delay characterization of all
the channels and delay states are detailed in Supporting Information,
Sections S8.1-S8.2. Figure 3d displays the calculated beam patterns
corresponding to different number of channels at RF frequency,
f = 20 GHz. Different number of channels is selected at different
steering angles for obviously comparison. The beamwidth has an

respectively.
Reconﬁgurable waveform and frequency spectrum generation
Tunable microwave photonic ﬁlters (MPFs) are crucial for enhancing
the performance, ﬂexibility, and reliability of modern communication
and sensing systems13,20. To demonstrate this function, the processor is
conﬁgured as a transversal tapped delay line, as shown in Fig. 4a. The
input RF signal ﬁrst modulates the equally spaced wavelength channels
with a 200 GHz frequency spacing (Δλ = 1.6 nm) via EO modulation.
The following input DERs array works as an on-chip waveshaper to
select the target wavelength. The shaped signals are then transmitted
through the TDL array to acquire different delays. The delayed signals
are then combined and amplitude-controlled by the output DER array
before being received by the PD. The transfer function of a transversal

Discussion
In summary, a versatile parallel signal processor with a scalable silicon
photonic chip has been demonstrated successfully. It comprises two
pair of DER-based (de)multiplexers, and optical-switch-based TDL to
control the signal in multiple optical dimensions. Additionally, utilizing
ultra-low-loss silicon waveguides with a waveguide loss of 0.14 dB/cm
and calibration-free MZI optical switch, the overall loss and chip pro-
gramming efforts are greatly reduced. The present versatile parallel
signal processor has been conﬁgured for realizing versatile advanced
functionalities, including accurate microwave reception, narrowband
microwave ﬁltering, wide-bandwidth arbitrary waveform generation
and high-speed parallel optical computing. The successful demon-
stration of these applications validates our chip design and imple-
mentation methods, paving the way for high-performance photonic
integrated circuits suitable for practical use.
The primary beneﬁt of this versatile parallel signal processor is its
scalability. The device can accommodate more parallel channels as the
overall loss is determined by a single channel. The footprint is also
optimized through the compact design of waveguide spirals and
optical switches, while minimizing the thermal crosstalk on the chip.
Additionally, the delay range in each channel can be extended with the
help of ultra-low-loss silicon waveguides. Our recent work demon-
strated the longest silicon delay line with a dynamic range of 5120 ps
and a ﬁne resolution of 10 ps using ultra-low-loss silicon waveguides57.
These extended parallel channels and time delays enable powerful
signal processing and advanced functions, such as a large-scale
beamforming array with a 100 MHz BW and58 and AI imaging
processing27.

Another advantage of this architecture is its simplicity in con-
ﬁguration. Optical switch-based programmable processors typically
require complex calibration (thousands of iterations) and numerous
testing elements if phase errors are random. Some specialized
approaches for auto-routing and self-conﬁguration have garnered
signiﬁcant attention7,39,40,59. These methods can effectively and
accurately achieve the target functionalities, and have been adopted
in commercial products60, but they may require additional time for
programming. Here, calibration-free MZI optical switches based on
broadened techniques are utilized, with switching states controlled
by a 0/3.8 V power supply. The current design eliminates the need
for careful calibration of most tuning elements, enabling the system
to efﬁciently manage complex signal-processing tasks. In addition,
the device controls amplitude, wavelength, and time delay using
distinct sections. This design is signiﬁcantly easier to conﬁgure than
controlling the light path by programming numerous optical
switches.

power consumption, integrating EO-effect optical switches to further

employing uniform power splitting couplers42 to increase the ER.
With the versatility of these technologies, large-scale programmable
silicon signal processor systems will provide a mass-productive and
cost-effective solution for a wide range of optoelectronics applica-
tions, thereby driving forward the next generation of silicon inte-
grated photonics.
Methods
Chip fabrication and assembly process
The proposed versatile parallel signal processer and corresponding
testing devices were fabricated at the MPW foundry (Advanced Micro
Foundry) with the standard processes. More details can be found in
Supporting information, Section S1. The chip was ﬁxed onto a copper
chuck employing thermal epoxy. The wire bonding process was used
to provide electrical connections between the chip and the printed
circuit board (PCB). Inverse taper edge couplers are used to achieve a
low-loss (1.8 dB/face) and broadband (>100 nm) horizontal ﬁber-chip
coupling. A ﬁber array with a pitch distance of 127 μm was aligned and
ﬁxed to the on-chip edge coupler array. A thermo-electric cooler (TEC)
had also been packaged to stabilize the chip to the ambient
temperature.
Device simulation
The ﬁnite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method was used to per-
form the physical simulations of the edge coupler, DERs, Euler-curve
tapered S-bend and optical MZI switch. The ﬁnite-difference fre-
quency-domain (FDFD) method was utilized to calculate the mode
proﬁle. The scattering losses of the waveguide surface and sidewall
were calculated with the three-dimensional volume current method
which is detailed in Supporting Information, Section S3.1.
